solution.concept_anchor: 5th vs 6th Schedule comparative governance features

statement_analysis.statement: In Fifth Schedule areas, tribal communities are represented through the Tribes Advisory Council which has a constitutional composition of not more than 20 members; in Sixth Schedule areas, Autonomous District Councils have elected membership not exceeding 30.
statement_analysis.reason: TAC: up to 20 members with 3/4 ST representation. ADC: up to 30 elected + 4 nominated — both figures are constitutionally correct.

statement_analysis.statement: PESA (1996) applies to both Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas, empowering Gram Sabhas in tribal areas across all northeastern states covered under either schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: PESA applies only to 5th Schedule areas — it explicitly does not apply to 6th Schedule areas. The northeastern states under the 6th Schedule (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) are outside PESA's scope.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor has the power to direct that a Central or State law shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, whereas under the Sixth Schedule, the Governor must obtain the concurrence of the District Council before modifying the application of laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Under the 6th Schedule, there is no requirement for the Governor to obtain District Council concurrence before exercising law-modification powers — the Governor acts independently, though ADC legislative acts need Governor's assent.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sixth Schedule provides for both District Councils and Regional Councils, while the Fifth Schedule provides only for the Tribes Advisory Council as the representative tribal body.
statement_analysis.reason: The 6th Schedule creates a two-tier structure (District Councils + Regional Councils), while the 5th Schedule creates only the TAC — this is an accurate structural comparison.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 4 as correct may lose focus and not critically examine Statement 3, which sounds plausible given the Governor's supervisory role over ADCs.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: TAC up to 20 members; ADC up to 30 elected + 4 nominated — both correct numbers. Statement 1 correct.
Statement 2: PESA explicitly does not apply to 6th Schedule areas — Statement 2 incorrect.
Statement 3: The Governor under the 6th Schedule does NOT need District Council concurrence before modifying law application — this is an invented requirement. Statement 3 incorrect.
Statement 4: 6th Schedule has District Councils + Regional Councils; 5th Schedule has only TAC — correct structural comparison. Statement 4 correct.

Two statements correct (1 and 4) — select option (b). Wait, options: (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Statements 1 and 4 correct = two correct → option (b). But reviewing the solution, correct_option is (a). Re-examine: Statement 1 correct, Statement 4 correct = 2 correct = option (b). Correcting correct_option to (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the sophisticated trap — it sounds like a logical balance to the Governor's extensive unilateral powers in 5th Schedule areas. Students who perceive that 6th Schedule offers more autonomy to tribal bodies may assume the Governor needs to consult or obtain concurrence from ADCs before modifying laws. In reality, the Governor's powers in 6th Schedule areas are supervisory (assent, reservation for President) rather than dependent on ADC concurrence.
solution.final_explanation:
The 5th and 6th Schedule represent two different constitutional philosophies for tribal governance — executive protection versus legislative autonomy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The compositional figures are constitutionally precise. TAC: up to 20 members with 3/4 ST representation. ADC: up to 30 elected + up to 4 nominated members.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: PESA explicitly covers only 5th Schedule areas. The 10 states with PESA coverage are all mainland states — no northeastern 6th Schedule state is covered.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: There is no constitutional requirement for the Governor to obtain District Council concurrence before modifying law application in 6th Schedule areas. Governor's powers are exercised independently; it is ADC laws that need the Governor's assent, not the other way.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 6th Schedule creates a two-tier representative structure (District + Regional Councils), while the 5th Schedule creates only the TAC as the representative body.

Value Addition:
• The Regional Council tier in the 6th Schedule accommodates intra-district tribal plurality — each significant tribe can have its own Regional Council.
• TAC's advisory-only nature makes it institutionally weaker despite being constitutionally created.
• Understanding both Schedules' governance architectures is essential for comparative tribal policy questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Governor's regulation-making power and Presidential assent under 5th Schedule
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because it correctly pairs Governor with annual report but incorrectly states the report goes to the state legislature — students who know governors report somewhere may not precisely recall whether it is the President or the legislature.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Governor submits the annual report on Scheduled Areas administration to the President, not the state legislature — the pair is incorrectly matched.
Eliminate option (c): The Governor's regulations under the 5th Schedule require the assent of the President (not the state cabinet or Chief Minister) — the pair is incorrect.
Eliminate option (d): The power to declare Scheduled Areas belongs to the President, not the Governor — this pair is incorrectly matched.
Accept option (b): Governor's power to make regulations for peace and good governance in Scheduled Areas paired with the requirement of Presidential assent — this is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits ambiguity about accountability mechanisms — Governors routinely submit reports to both state legislatures and the Centre in different contexts. The 5th Schedule annual report going to the President (not the state legislature) is a precise fact that requires specific recall, not general intuition about governmental accountability.
solution.final_explanation:
The Fifth Schedule creates a direct Governor-President relationship for Scheduled Areas administration, bypassing the state legislature in certain accountability mechanisms.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Governor submits the annual report on Scheduled Areas to the President, not the state legislature. This is a direct Centre-Governor accountability link.
• Option (b) — Correct: Under the 5th Schedule, the Governor can make regulations for the peace and good governance of Scheduled Areas. However, such regulations require Presidential assent before coming into force — not the state cabinet's approval.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Presidential assent (not the state cabinet's assent) is required for Governor's regulations under the 5th Schedule. The state cabinet's role in this specific power is excluded.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The power to declare Scheduled Areas belongs to the President, not the Governor. The Governor is consulted, but the declaratory power is presidential.

Value Addition:
• The Presidential assent requirement for Governor's regulations creates a direct Union oversight over 5th Schedule governance — state governments have limited ability to modify this.
• The Governor's 5th Schedule powers are exercised independently, not necessarily on the state cabinet's advice — a unique constitutional exception.
• The annual report mechanism is a constitutional accountability tool rarely invoked effectively in practice.

solution.concept_anchor: High Court jurisdiction and ADC court powers under 6th Schedule

statement_analysis.statement: District and Regional Councils under the Sixth Schedule can constitute village courts to try suits and cases between parties who are all members of Scheduled Tribes.
statement_analysis.reason: The 6th Schedule explicitly empowers District and Regional Councils to constitute village courts (or courts of a similar nature) to try such cases — this is a core judicial power under the Schedule.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor has the power, under the Sixth Schedule, to exclude or restrict the jurisdiction of the High Court over the courts constituted by District or Regional Councils.
statement_analysis.reason: The 6th Schedule enables the Governor, by notification, to exclude or limit the jurisdiction of High Courts with respect to suits and cases between tribals tried by council courts.

statement_analysis.statement: Village courts constituted by District Councils under the Sixth Schedule have jurisdiction to try criminal cases including all offences under the Indian Penal Code if the accused is a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
statement_analysis.reason: Village court jurisdiction is limited to specified civil disputes and customary law matters — they do not have blanket jurisdiction over all IPC criminal offences merely because the accused is a tribal.

solution.strong_distractor: d — This is the correct answer, but the strong distractor is option (c) '1 and 3 only' which students who are uncertain about Statement 3 might choose, mixing the clearly correct Statement 1 with the false Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Village courts constituted by ADCs for inter-tribal disputes is an explicit 6th Schedule provision — correct.
Verify Statement 2: Governor's power to exclude/limit High Court jurisdiction over these courts is expressly provided — correct.

Reject Statement 3: Blanket criminal jurisdiction (all IPC offences) based solely on accused being tribal is not how 6th Schedule court jurisdiction is defined — the jurisdiction is subject-specific, not person-specific in this unlimited way.
Select option (d): only Statements 1 and 2 are correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the assumption that if courts are constituted for tribals, they should have comprehensive jurisdiction over cases involving tribals — including criminal matters. The 6th Schedule courts have specified subject jurisdiction, not blanket criminal jurisdiction. Criminal law in India remains primarily a Union subject, and ADC courts cannot substitute for regular criminal courts on all IPC offences.
solution.final_explanation:
The judicial powers under the 6th Schedule create a parallel court system for specified tribal disputes, operating alongside but distinct from the regular judicial hierarchy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: District and Regional Councils can constitute village courts (or courts of analogous nature) to try cases where all parties are Scheduled Tribe members — covering specified civil and customary law matters.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Governor has explicit power under the 6th Schedule to exclude the jurisdiction of High Courts over these council-constituted courts, by public notification. This is a significant constitutional departure from the normal High Court supervisory jurisdiction.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: ADC village courts do not have blanket criminal jurisdiction over all IPC offences involving tribal accused. Their jurisdiction is defined by the subject matters specified under the 6th Schedule — primarily customary law disputes between tribal parties.

Value Addition:
• The High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226 for fundamental rights enforcement cannot be fully excluded even by Governor's order under the 6th Schedule.
• ADC courts applying customary tribal law represent one of India's constitutional acknowledgments of legal pluralism.
• The power to dissolve District and Regional Councils under the 6th Schedule also rests with the Governor — subject to Presidential confirmation.

solution.concept_anchor: Legislative and policy milestones in 5th Schedule tribal governance
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it correctly positions PESA but reverses the order of the Samatha judgment and the Forest Rights Act, exploiting the closeness of dates (1997 vs 2006) and assuming FRA came before Samatha.
elimination_logic: Anchor: The Constitution with 5th and 6th Schedules was enacted in 1949/1950 — this is the foundational event.
PESA was enacted in December 1996 — second in sequence.
The Samatha judgment was delivered in 1997 — immediately after PESA.
The Forest Rights Act was enacted in 2006 — last in sequence.
Correct order: Constitution (1950) → PESA (1996) → Samatha judgment (1997) → Forest Rights Act (2006) → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap targets the year proximity between PESA (1996), Samatha (1997), and the general knowledge that both preceded the Forest Rights Act (2006). Students who confuse Samatha's year (1997 — just after PESA) or misplace FRA before Samatha will select options (a), (c), or (d). The one-year gap between PESA and Samatha is a deliberate precision test.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of tribal rights jurisprudence and legislation in post-independence India followed a clear sequential pattern.

Correct chronological sequence:
1. Fifth Schedule (Constitution, 1950): The foundational constitutional framework for Scheduled Areas and tribal governance.
2. PESA, 1996: Extended Part IX (Panchayats) to 5th Schedule areas, empowering Gram Sabhas with specific rights over natural resources and local governance.
3. Samatha Judgment, 1997: The Supreme Court held that private non-tribal entities cannot receive mining leases in Scheduled Areas — a landmark expansion of tribal land protection.
4. Forest Rights Act, 2006: Granted individual and community forest rights to Scheduled Tribes and forest dwellers, addressing historical dispossession.

Wrong options fail because:
• Placing Samatha before PESA ignores that PESA (1996) preceded the judgment (1997).
• Placing FRA before Samatha confuses the decade gap between them.

Value Addition:
• The Samatha judgment was a direct judicial response to exploitation occurring despite the 5th Schedule's protective framework.
• PESA and FRA together constitute the two major statutory pillars of post-1990 tribal rights expansion.
• The Bhuria Committee Report (1994-95) recommended what eventually became PESA.

solution.concept_anchor: Ladakh 6th Schedule demand and 100th Amendment Act 2015

statement_analysis.statement: The 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 pertained to the acquisition of certain territories by India and transfer of certain territories to Bangladesh, arising from the Land Boundary Agreement.
statement_analysis.reason: The 100th Amendment implemented the 1974 Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) and its 2011 Protocol between India and Bangladesh, exchanging enclaves and defining the land boundary.

statement_analysis.statement: Ladakh has been formally included under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution through a Presidential Order following its reorganisation as a Union Territory in 2019.
statement_analysis.reason: Despite strong demands from Ladakh tribal bodies and political parties, Ladakh has NOT been brought under the 6th Schedule. The demand remains pending — no Presidential Order or constitutional amendment has been made to this effect.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both statements deal with recent constitutional changes, and the high-profile nature of Ladakh's reorganisation (2019) makes students assume follow-up 6th Schedule inclusion occurred.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 100th Amendment (2015) is accurately described — it implemented the India-Bangladesh land boundary agreement. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Ladakh's inclusion under the 6th Schedule is a PENDING DEMAND — it has not been implemented through any Presidential Order or amendment. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the very visible political demand for Ladakh's inclusion under the 6th Schedule, which received significant media attention after Ladakh became a UT in 2019. Students who followed the news may confuse the demand with implementation. This is a classic plausible-fabrication trap — the demand is real, the implementation is not. UPSC frequently tests the boundary between announced intentions and actual constitutional changes.
solution.final_explanation:
Both statements deal with significant recent constitutional developments — one completed, one still a pending demand.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 100th Constitutional Amendment Act (2015) gave effect to the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement, resolving a decades-old dispute by exchanging enclaves and adverse possessions. Territories were formally transferred between the two countries, requiring a constitutional amendment since it affected Indian territory.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Ladakh's inclusion under the 6th Schedule is a sustained political demand made by Ladakhi tribal representatives, Buddhist and Muslim communities, and various political parties following the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act (2019) that made Ladakh a UT. However, as of the time of this question, no Presidential Order or constitutional amendment has extended the 6th Schedule to Ladakh.

Value Addition:
• The 100th Amendment involved actual territorial changes — India received 111 Bangladeshi enclaves and Bangladesh received 51 Indian enclaves.
• Ladakh's demand focuses specifically on 6th Schedule inclusion for its tribal populations in Leh and Kargil districts.
• The Leh Hill Development Council (LAHDC) currently administers Leh — but this is a statutory body, not a 6th Schedule ADC.

solution.concept_anchor: Non-application of 6th Schedule to Nagaland and Manipur

statement_analysis.statement: Nagaland is excluded from the Sixth Schedule because its tribal areas are governed under the specific protections of Article 371(A), which overrides the need for the Sixth Schedule framework.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 371(A) provides Nagaland with special protection for Naga customary law, making a parallel 6th Schedule structure redundant — this is the correct constitutional explanation for Nagaland's exclusion.

statement_analysis.statement: Manipur's hill areas are governed under the Sixth Schedule through the Hill Areas Committee constituted under Article 371(C), which functions as an Autonomous District Council for the hill districts.
statement_analysis.reason: The Hill Areas Committee under Article 371(C) is NOT an ADC under the 6th Schedule — it is a legislative committee within the Manipur state legislature. Manipur's hill areas are not under the 6th Schedule.

statement_analysis.statement: Arunachal Pradesh is excluded from the Sixth Schedule because its tribal population follows a lifestyle and customary governance system that the Constitution sought to preserve through the special protection under Article 371(H).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 371(H) relates to the special responsibility of the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh regarding law and order — it does not specifically address customary governance preservation as the basis for exclusion from the 6th Schedule. The exact constitutional rationale for Arunachal's exclusion is its historically different tribal administration, not Article 371(H)'s specific content.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Statement 2 contains recognizable correct elements (Hill Areas Committee, Article 371C, Manipur) — students who know all three entities exist may miss the false causal link between the HAC and the 6th Schedule.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Article 371(A) protects Naga customary law — this is the correct explanation for Nagaland's exclusion from the 6th Schedule. Statement 1 is CORRECT (not incorrect).
Statement 2: The Hill Areas Committee under Article 371(C) is a parliamentary committee within Manipur's legislature — NOT an ADC under the 6th Schedule. Statement 2 is INCORRECT.

Statement 3: Article 371(H) deals with the Governor's special responsibility over law and order in Arunachal Pradesh — the characterisation of 371(H) as specifically preserving customary governance is an overstatement. Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Select option (c): Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the master conflation trap — it merges the Hill Areas Committee (a real constitutional body under Article 371C) with Autonomous District Councils (a 6th Schedule body) into a single false composite. Students who know both entities exist may not notice that the statement falsely calls the HAC an ADC. The HAC is a committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly, not an autonomous council with legislative powers — a fundamental constitutional distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
The exclusions from the 6th Schedule among northeastern states reflect distinct constitutional arrangements rather than a uniform rationale.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nagaland's exclusion from the 6th Schedule is correctly explained by Article 371(A), which provides comprehensive protection for Naga customary law, religious practices, and social systems — making a separate ADC framework unnecessary.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Hill Areas Committee in Manipur is constituted under Article 371(C) as a committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly to deal with bills affecting hill areas. It is NOT an Autonomous District Council under the 6th Schedule, does not have independent legislative powers, and functions as a parliamentary committee, not an autonomous governing body.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 371(H) gives the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh a special responsibility regarding law and order — it does not specifically frame the province of customary governance preservation. The characterisation in Statement 3 overinterprets 371(H)'s actual constitutional content.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland's special status under 371(A) is among the most comprehensive special state provisions — covering all Naga customary law and social practices.
• Manipur has a unique dual tribal governance: hill districts have the HAC under 371(C), and Manipur's relatively small tribal areas are also covered by some ADC-like arrangements.
• Only four states currently have 6th Schedule coverage: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 244A unimplemented status and political reasons
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may see Article 244A as a logical constitutional response to tribal demands (A) and assume the two-thirds majority requirement is the reason it remains unimplemented (R), accepting both as true and causally linked.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Article 244A (inserted by the 22nd Amendment, 1969) remains unimplemented despite being a constitutional provision for over five decades.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. Article 244A requires Parliament to pass a law with the additional condition of a two-thirds majority in the Assam Assembly — NOT a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament. The Reason as stated describes an incorrect procedure (conflating it with Article 368 special majority requirements).
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect (wrong procedural description), the answer must be (c): A correct but R incorrect.
Correct option is (c), not (d). Correcting: correct_option should be 'c'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Reason statement describes a constitutional amendment procedure (two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament) — conflating Article 244A's special procedure with Article 368. Article 244A requires a Parliament-enacted law plus a two-thirds resolution of the Assam Assembly — not a special majority in Parliament itself. Students who know '244A requires some special majority' but are imprecise about whose majority may accept R as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 244A is a unique constitutional provision that illustrates the difference between constitutional authorization and political implementation.

Assertion (A) is correct: Despite being inserted in 1969 through the 22nd Amendment, Article 244A has never been implemented. No autonomous state within Assam has been created under this provision — making it a dormant constitutional clause for over 50 years.

Reason (R) is incorrect: Article 244A does NOT require a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament. The procedure requires Parliament to enact a law (through ordinary legislative process), but with the additional condition that the Assam Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority. The Reason incorrectly describes the procedure by attributing the special majority requirement to Parliament rather than the Assam Assembly.

Since A is correct but R is incorrect, the answer is option (c).

Value Addition:
• The 22nd Amendment (1969) was specifically designed for the United Mikir and North Cachar Hills — but political negotiations never concluded successfully.
• Article 244A is distinct from Article 3 (creation of new states) — it creates sub-state autonomous structures, not full states.
• The Bodo Accord (2003) and the subsequent BTC represent an alternative path to addressing similar aspirations through the 6th Schedule framework rather than Article 244A.

solution.concept_anchor: ADC powers across legislative, executive, and financial domains
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it correctly matches grants-in-aid but swaps land revenue and mineral royalties, exploiting the confusion between the State's Consolidated Fund (grants) and revenue from mineral licensing.
elimination_logic: Match A: The power to assess and collect land revenue within autonomous districts is an ADC financial power — A matches with 3.
Match B: Grants-in-aid are drawn from the Consolidated Fund of the State — B matches with 1.
Match C: Royalties from licenses for mineral exploration/extraction constitute ADC revenue — C matches with 4.
Match D: The power to establish and maintain markets is an ADC executive power — D matches with 2.
Only option (b) — A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — correctly reflects all four matches.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets the distinction between the Consolidated Fund of the State (grants-in-aid source) and the revenue mechanisms of land and mineral royalties. Students who associate 'Consolidated Fund' with Union resources (Consolidated Fund of India) may misplace the grants item. Similarly, those who blur land revenue and mineral royalties — both being revenue items — may swap A and C in their matching.
solution.final_explanation:
The financial and executive powers of ADCs under the 6th Schedule cover multiple domains that must be precisely categorised.

Correct matches:
• A (Land revenue assessment and collection) — 3: ADCs have the constitutional power to levy, assess, and collect land revenue from land within their autonomous districts — a direct revenue-generating power.
• B (Grants-in-aid to ADCs) — 1: Grants-in-aid to ADCs are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the State — these are budgetary transfers from the state government to support ADC administration.
• C (Royalties from mineral licensing) — 4: ADCs receive royalties from licenses they grant for extraction of minor minerals — this is a revenue share from resource exploitation within the district.
• D (Market establishment and management) — 2: The power to establish, construct, and manage markets falls within ADC executive powers — a local economic governance function.

Value Addition:
• ADCs maintain a District Fund (and Regional Fund) for managing their receipts and expenditures — constitutionally prescribed fiscal structures.
• The dual revenue system (ADC revenue + state grants) makes ADCs financially semi-autonomous but dependent.
• Major mineral revenues remain with the Union and state governments — ADC royalty rights are restricted to minor minerals.

solution.concept_anchor: PESA enactment year and the Bhuria Committee basis
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 1992 is the year of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (Panchayati Raj), and students who associate PESA with the Panchayati Raj framework naturally associate it with 1992 rather than 1996.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): 1992 is the year of the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments introducing Part IX and Part IXA — PESA was enacted separately in 1996.
Eliminate option (c): 1994 is the year of the Bhuria Committee report recommending extension of panchayat provisions to tribal areas — but PESA itself came in 1996.
Eliminate option (d): 2006 is the year of the Forest Rights Act — a different tribal rights legislation.
Accept option (a): PESA was enacted in December 1996 — correctly matched with option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1992-1996 temporal proximity is the core trap. The 73rd Amendment (1992) is deeply associated in student memory with Panchayati Raj reform, and since PESA extends Part IX to tribal areas, students instinctively link it to 1992. The four-year gap between the constitutional amendment and the tribal extension legislation (PESA) is a precise recall test that exploits this association.
solution.final_explanation:
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act is a landmark legislation extending decentralised governance to tribal areas.

• Option (a) — Correct: PESA was enacted in 1996. It extended the Panchayati Raj framework to Scheduled Areas under the 5th Schedule with modifications to protect tribal autonomy.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 1992 is the year of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment introducing Part IX (Panchayats) — the very legislation that PESA later extended to tribal areas. PESA came four years later.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 1994 saw the Bhuria Committee report that recommended the tribal extension of panchayat provisions — but the actual legislation followed in 1996.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 2006 is the year of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act — a different statute.

Value Addition:
• The Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee (1994-95) was the parliamentary committee whose recommendations became the basis for PESA.
• PESA was enacted specifically because the 73rd Amendment's Part IX was not applicable to Scheduled Areas under Article 243M.
• PESA is sometimes called the 'Constitution for tribal India' — reflecting its transformative intent for local self-governance in tribal areas.

solution.concept_anchor: Samatha judgment application to government corporations in Scheduled Areas
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'State-owned corporations can mine in Scheduled Areas with Gram Sabha consent' sounds like a reasonable compromise position that combines two known principles — State ownership and Gram Sabha consent — but misrepresents what Samatha actually permits.
elimination_logic: Identify the framework: A 5th Schedule Scheduled Area — Samatha judgment (1997) applies.
Eliminate option (a): The Samatha judgment does not require parliamentary amendment before state-owned mining; it sets conditions for permissibility.

Eliminate option (b): Samatha did not simply subject State corporations to Gram Sabha consent — it was more complex: State Mining Corporations are permissible but must contribute to a Tribal Development Fund; private companies are prohibited.
Eliminate option (d): Complete prohibition on state-owned corporation mining is not what Samatha held — state entities with specific conditions were permitted.

Accept option (c): The Samatha judgment held that State-owned mining corporations may operate in Scheduled Areas but must earmark specified proportions of net profits for tribal development funds — this conditional permissibility is the correct reading.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) uses a tempting synthesis — State ownership plus Gram Sabha consent sounds like a progressive democratic safeguard consistent with PESA and Samatha. But the Samatha ruling did not impose a Gram Sabha consent requirement on State mining corporations — it imposed a financial benefit-sharing condition (Tribal Development Fund) as the legitimising condition. Students who layer PESA's Gram Sabha consent requirement onto Samatha's state-entity exception will choose option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Samatha judgment (1997) is a nuanced ruling that did not impose a blanket prohibition on all mining in Scheduled Areas — it established a differentiated framework.

In this scenario, the State Mining Development Corporation is a State-owned entity, not a private company. Under Samatha:

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliamentary amendment is not required to permit State corporation mining — Samatha addressed the existing legal framework.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Samatha did not make State corporation mining contingent on Gram Sabha consent alone. The PESA-Gram Sabha requirement and the Samatha conditions operate differently.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Samatha judgment held that State-owned corporations can engage in mining in Scheduled Areas, but with mandatory conditions including earmarking a portion of net profits (20% was discussed) into a Tribal Development Fund for the benefit of the affected tribal community.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Complete prohibition applies to private non-tribal companies and corporations — not to State-owned mining entities.

Value Addition:
• Samatha also held that even government itself cannot transfer land in Scheduled Areas to non-tribals for commercial purposes without meeting constitutional requirements.
• The Tribal Development Fund requirement was intended to ensure mining did not impoverish tribal communities whose land was being used.
• The MMDR (Amendment) Act, 2015 further strengthened benefit-sharing for project-affected tribes in Scheduled Areas.
